cases.input:
What is this bill really trying to do? I only skimmed it.

H.R. 4417, "Consumer Data Transparency and Security Act of 2027" (fictional). Introduced 2027-03-09 by Rep. Marlene Okafor-Tran (D-OR), cosponsored by Rep. Dale Whitcombe (R-OH). Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

Sec. 2. Findings. Congress finds that consumers lack visibility into how their personal data is bought and sold.
Sec. 3. Disclosure. Each covered entity shall, on request, disclose to a consumer the categories of third parties that received that consumer's personal data in the prior 24 months.
Sec. 4. Definitions. 'Covered entity' means any person that collects personal data on more than 500,000 consumers in a calendar year and derives more than 50 percent of annual revenue from the sale of personal data. 'Personal data' does not include data that has been pseudonymized by the covered entity.
Sec. 5. Security. A covered entity shall maintain reasonable security practices, as determined by the Secretary of Commerce by rule, within 36 months of enactment.
Sec. 6. Preemption. This Act supersedes any provision of State law that relates to the collection, processing, sale, or disclosure of personal data, whether or not such law provides greater protection.
Sec. 7. Enforcement. The Attorney General may bring a civil action. Nothing in this Act creates a private right of action. Civil penalties shall not exceed $2,500 per violation and shall not exceed $1,000,000 in aggregate per entity per year.
Sec. 8. Safe harbor. A covered entity that adopts a self-certified compliance program approved by an industry standards body recognized by the Secretary shall be deemed in compliance with Sections 3 and 5.
Sec. 9. Effective date. This Act takes effect 48 months after enactment.
cases.expects: Delivers the bill's metadata, a short summary, and separate lists of overt goals (consumer disclosure, security) and covert ones that the text actually supports, such as the 50 percent revenue threshold excluding most brokers, the pseudonymization carve-out, broad state preemption, capped penalties, self-certified safe harbor and the long delay, each tied to its section. Ends with an opinionated verdict on how much of the bill is genuine versus self-serving, and invents no motive the text does not show.

cases.input:
Run analyze bill on this. I want the overt goals and the covert ones, and your verdict.

S. 902, "Resilient Grid Modernization Act" (fictional). Introduced 2027-05-14 by Sen. Tobias Heller-Nguyen (I-VT). Referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

Title I. Grid Hardening. Sec. 101 authorizes $4.2 billion over five years for transmission upgrades in regions designated by the Secretary of Energy as 'high-risk'. Sec. 102 directs the Secretary to publish designation criteria within 18 months.
Title II. Cybersecurity. Sec. 201 requires operators of 'critical grid assets' to report cyber incidents to the Department within 72 hours. Sec. 202 establishes that reports are exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act and may not be used in any regulatory enforcement action.
Title III. Permitting. Sec. 301 establishes an expedited review track of 90 days for projects funded under Title I. Sec. 302 provides that judicial review of any such project must be filed within 30 days of the final agency action, and that no court may enjoin construction pending review.
Title IV. Workforce. Sec. 401 authorizes $300 million for apprenticeship programs administered by 'qualified consortia', defined as groups including at least one entity with a prior Department of Energy award exceeding $50 million.
Title V. General. Sec. 501 establishes a Grid Advisory Council of 11 members appointed by the Secretary, of whom at least 6 must be representatives of regulated utilities. Sec. 502 repeals Section 14(c) of the Transmission Siting Review Act (fictional), which required public hearings in affected counties.
cases.expects: Delivers bill metadata, a tight summary, and clearly separated overt goals (hardening, incident reporting, workforce) and covert ones grounded in the text, such as FOIA and enforcement immunity for incident reports, no injunctions and a 30-day challenge window, the qualified-consortia definition favoring incumbents, utility-majority advisory council and repeal of county hearings. Closes with a firm opinionated judgement on how much is straightforward versus ulterior.

cases.input:
Someone sent me this scrap from a bill, no title, no sponsor, pasted from a PDF with the formatting wrecked. Tell me what it's doing and what's buried in it. I know it's thin.

...(c) PARAGRAPH (4) of subsection (b) of section 7 of the Digital Services Integrity Act (fictional) is amended by striking 'knowingly' and inserting 'with actual knowledge, as established by clear and convincing evidence,'. (d) Sec. 7(f) is amended by adding at the end: '(3) A provider acting in good faith under this section shall be immune from liability for any content removal, account suspension, or data retention decision, notwithstanding any other provision of law.' (e) TECHNICAL AND CONFORMING AMENDMENTS.--Section 12(a) is amended by striking '180 days' and inserting '5 years'. Section 19 is repealed. (f) EFFECTIVE DATE.--The amendments made by this section shall apply to conduct occurring before, on, or after the date of enactment. [page 31 of 212] ...

Note: header says 'Rep. ___ (R-__)' and the date is cut off.
cases.expects: States plainly that sponsor, date and title are missing rather than guessing, then reads only what the fragment supports: the overt change is liability protection for providers, while the covert effects include the near-impossible actual-knowledge standard, blanket immunity overriding other law, the 180-day-to-5-year change whose subject is unknown, an unexplained repeal of Section 19 and retroactive application. Flags what cannot be judged without the base statute, and gives a hedged but direct verdict instead of inventing intent.
